subject: Business Models
title: Pay What You Want
description: A 60-second lesson on Pay What You Want.

hook.text: Radiohead released In Rainbows in 2007 with a 'pay what you want' price. Most people paid nothing. It still worked.

buildup.text: Pay-what-you-want lets customers set the price. It relies on goodwill, social pressure, and perceived value.

discovery.text: Panera's pay-what-you-want cafes found that 60% paid full price, 20% paid more, and 20% paid less or nothing.

twist.text: Panera closed all pay-what-you-want locations by 2021. The model attracted too many free-riders over time.

climax.text: Pay-what-you-want works for digital goods with zero marginal cost, but fails for physical products with real costs.

punchline.text: Name your price: some pay more, most pay less. Digital wins, physical fails.

quiz.question: Why did Panera close its pay-what-you-want cafes?
options: Too many free-riders undermined the economics over time

details.summary: Pay-what-you-want pricing lets customers choose how much they pay, including potentially nothing. When used strategically with social pressure, suggested prices, and charitable components, PWYW can generate higher revenue than fixed pricing for certain products.
details.whyItMatters: PWYW reveals customer valuation and builds goodwill. Radiohead's PWYW album and Humble Bundle's gaming platform showed that trust-based pricing can work commercially when combined with social dynamics and compelling products.
takeaways: Customers choose their own price, sometimes exceeding the market rate
Social pressure and suggested minimums increase average payment amounts
Works best for digital goods with near-zero marginal cost of distribution

faq.question: When does pay-what-you-want pricing actually work?
faq.answer: PWYW works best for digital goods with low marginal costs, products with strong emotional connection, contexts with social visibility where others see what you paid, and when bundled with charitable giving that motivates higher payments.

faq.question: What prevents everyone from paying nothing?
faq.answer: Social norms, reciprocity instincts, fairness perceptions, anchoring from suggested prices, and guilt. Research shows most people pay something, and adding a charitable component significantly increases average payments above zero.
